# BugOut website, full text

> BugOut: Offline Survival Kit is an iPhone app for emergency preparedness that works with no internet. It carries 68 field guides, including the U.S. Army Survival Manual (FM 21-76), plus Survival Essentials (the core method for 56 emergencies), 7 step-by-step disaster scenarios with gear checklists, your own gear lists, phone sensor tools, and Wally, an AI survival assistant that runs on the iPhone itself.

# The survival app that works with no signal.

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/
Updated: 2026-11-09

BugOut puts 68 field guides, the U.S. Army Survival Manual, step-by-step disaster plans and Wally, an AI survival assistant that runs on your iPhone, in your pocket. No internet, no account.

## Ask a survival question. Get an answer without a signal.

Wally is an AI survival assistant built into BugOut. Ask in plain words and it answers from BugOut's own library, leading with the core method from Survival Essentials and showing the passages each answer is based on.

- **Works anywhere:** in airplane mode, in the backcountry, in a blackout. Wally runs entirely on your iPhone.
- **Private by design:** your questions never leave your phone. No account, no tracking.
- **Grounded in the library:** answers come from the CDC, FEMA and U.S. Army material in the app, not the open internet. Like any AI, Wally can make mistakes, so check the source before you rely on an answer.
- **Which iPhone models:** written answers need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro or newer, iOS 26). Other iPhone models get the most relevant passages from the guides. Wally is part of BugOut Pro.

How do I make water safe to drink?

Wally, AI answer

1. Let cloudy water settle, then pour clear water through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter [1]
2. Boil water for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 feet) [1]
3. If boiling isn't possible, use plain, unscented bleach: 8 drops per gallon of clear water, 16 drops if cloudy; stir and wait 30 minutes before drinking [1]

**[1] Survival Essentials**Make water safe to drink: boil, bleach or purify

## A survival library that lives on your phone

Everything is stored on your iPhone, so it's there when the network, the power or the trail runs out.

### Survival Essentials, the master guide

The core method for 56 emergencies, from severe bleeding, CPR and choking to house fires, floods and tornadoes. One short, step-by-step section each, written from CDC, FEMA and U.S. Army guidance.

68

### Field guides and manuals

The U.S. Army Survival Manual (FM 21-76), Army first aid and land navigation manuals, cold-weather and Marine Corps survival courses, and 36 original guides on power outages, storms, water and more. All free and searchable.

7

### Disaster scenarios with checklists

Power grid down, nuclear event, pandemic, purifying water in a city, building a kit, the first 72 hours, and surviving with children or older adults. Each has a step-by-step plan and a gear checklist.

0

### Bars of signal needed

Guides, checklists, your own gear lists and the phone's sensors all work offline: GPS coordinates, battery time-to-empty, plus a compass and barometer with Pro.

## BugOut at a glance

What it is
:   An emergency preparedness and survival guide app for iPhone that works with no internet connection.

Platform
:   iPhone with iOS 16 or later, on the U.S. App Store.

Price
:   Free download. BugOut Pro is $6.99 a month or $54.99 a year.

Works offline
:   Yes. Guides, checklists, scenarios and sensor tools work with no signal and no account. Only buying or restoring Pro needs a connection.

What's inside
:   68 field guides, including the U.S. Army Survival Manual (FM 21-76); Survival Essentials, the core method for 56 emergencies in 12 topics; 7 disaster scenarios with gear checklists.

AI assistant
:   Ask Wally runs on the iPhone and shows the BugOut passages each answer is based on. Written answers need Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro or newer, iOS 26 or later). Part of BugOut Pro. Like any AI, it can make mistakes.

Sources
:   U.S. military field manuals, the CDC, EPA, FEMA and Ready.gov, the American Red Cross, the National Weather Service and the National Park Service.

Privacy
:   No account. Questions to Wally, your location and your lists stay on the phone; the only data collected is anonymous purchase history.

## Questions

Is there a survival app that works offline?

Yes. BugOut is built to work with no internet at all. The field guides, Survival Essentials, the disaster scenarios, your gear lists and the phone's GPS and battery tools all work in airplane mode, with no account. Only buying or restoring BugOut Pro needs a connection.

What is the best prepper app?

It depends on what you need it for. For getting through an emergency, look for an app that works offline, gives step-by-step instructions instead of long articles, and says where its advice comes from. BugOut was built around those three things. For alerts and shelter locations, pair it with the FEMA app or a NOAA weather radio, which need a signal or a broadcast.

Does Ask Wally need internet?

No. Wally runs entirely on your iPhone and answers from BugOut's own library, so it works with no signal and your questions never leave your phone. Written answers need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) on iOS 26 or later, once Apple Intelligence is turned on and has finished its one-time download. On other iPhone models, Wally shows the most relevant passages from the guides instead. Wally is part of BugOut Pro, and like any AI it can make mistakes, so check the source before you rely on an answer.

Is the U.S. Army Survival Manual included?

Yes. BugOut includes the U.S. Army Survival Manual (FM 21-76), along with the Army's first aid and map reading manuals and cold-weather and Marine Corps survival courses. They're free, searchable and stored on your phone.

Is BugOut free?

The download is free, and so are all the field guides, your own gear lists, two full scenarios (power grid down and nuclear event), the first method in each Survival Essentials topic, and the battery, GPS and connectivity tools. BugOut Pro ($6.99 a month or $54.99 a year) adds all 7 scenarios, all 56 Survival Essentials methods, Ask Wally, and the compass, barometer and daylight tracking.

Where does BugOut's information come from?

From public sources you can check: U.S. military field manuals, the CDC, EPA, FEMA and Ready.gov, the American Red Cross, the National Weather Service and the National Park Service. Survival Essentials lists the sources it was written from, and every Wally answer links to the BugOut passages it's based on. BugOut is a reference, not a substitute for training, so take a first-aid and CPR class too.

Which iPhone models does BugOut run on?

Any iPhone with iOS 16 or later. Ask Wally's written answers need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) on iOS 26 or later. BugOut is available on the U.S. App Store.

## Questions

### What is the first thing to do to prepare for an emergency?

Make a plan with your household: how you'll get warnings, where you'll shelter, where you'd go if you had to leave, and how you'll reach each other. Then store water, 1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days.

### What are the most important survival skills?

Knowing what to do first. Get away from immediate danger, stop severe bleeding, get out of the weather, then deal with water, signaling and food, in that order.

### Are these survival guides free?

Yes. Every guide and printable checklist on this page is free to read, print and share. The BugOut app, a free download for iPhone, carries a larger library that works with no signal.

### Where does the information come from?

Each guide is written from public guidance by agencies such as FEMA, the CDC, the EPA and the National Weather Service, and from the U.S. Army Survival Manual, and lists its sources at the end.

# Emergency preparedness: how to prepare for any disaster

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-preparedness/
Updated: 2026-11-09

Being prepared comes down to three things: a plan everyone in the house knows, supplies for several days, and a way to hear warnings. This guide walks through each one and links to a checklist for every step.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 9, 2026. Checked against FEMA (Ready.gov), CDC and National Weather Service guidance.

The short answer

Do three things, in this order. **Make a plan:** agree how you'll get warnings, where you'll shelter, where you'll go if you have to leave, and how you'll reach each other. **Build a kit:** at least 3 days of water (1 gallon per person per day), food that won't spoil, light, a radio, first aid and medicines. **Stay informed:** keep emergency alerts on and own a battery or hand-crank radio. The same three steps cover almost any disaster.

## What emergency preparedness means

Emergency preparedness, or disaster preparedness, is what you do before something goes wrong so that your household can stay safe and look after itself until help arrives or services come back. FEMA's planning assumes help may not reach everyone right away, so the aim is to cover your own basic needs for several days.

You don't need a different plan for every disaster. A power outage, a winter storm, a hurricane, a flood and an earthquake all come down to the same questions: do we stay or go, do we have water, food, light and medicine, and how do we find out what's happening?

## Step 0: Know what's likely where you live

- **Look up your county.** FEMA's National Risk Index rates every U.S. county and census tract for 18 natural hazards, from hurricanes and tornadoes to wildfire, earthquakes and winter weather.
- **Ask your local emergency management office** which events it plans for and where the evacuation routes and shelters are.

Your list shapes the details: hurricane country needs an evacuation plan, cold climates need a way to stay warm without power.

## Step 1: Make a family emergency plan

Ready.gov's planning steps start with questions to talk through with your household:

1. How will we get emergency alerts and warnings?
2. Where will we shelter at home, for a tornado, a storm or a chemical spill?
3. What's our evacuation route, and where would we go?
4. How will we reach each other if we're apart and phones are down?
5. Do we need to update our emergency supplies?

- Pick an out-of-town contact everyone can text. Texts often get through when calls don't.
- Choose two meeting places: one near home, one outside your neighborhood
- Write phone numbers on paper for every wallet and bag
- Plan for young children, older relatives, pets and anyone with medical needs
- Plan for medical devices that need electricity
- Learn how to shut off your water, gas and electricity
- Practice once, including walking or driving your evacuation route

## Step 2: Build an emergency kit

A home kit covers several days without power, water or stores. The core of FEMA's list:

- **Water:** 1 gallon per person per day. Store at least 3 days and work toward 2 weeks.
- **Food:** several days of food that needs no fridge and little or no cooking, plus a manual can opener.
- **Light and news:** a flashlight, extra batteries, and a battery or hand-crank radio.
- **Health:** a first-aid kit, prescription medicines and glasses.
- **Everything else:** a whistle, dust masks, basic tools, local maps, a phone charger with a backup battery, copies of documents and cash.

Our [emergency kit list](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-kit-list/) has the full checklist to print, and the [water calculator](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-water-calculator/) works out the amounts for your household. If you may have to leave home fast, pack a [bug out bag](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/bug-out-bag-list/) for each person, and keep a [kit in the car](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/car-emergency-kit/).

## Step 3: Stay informed

- Keep emergency alerts turned on in your phone's settings. Wireless Emergency Alerts reach capable phones automatically, with no sign-up. The National Weather Service uses them for tornado, flash flood, hurricane, tsunami and other warnings.
- Sign up for your county's local alert system
- Own a battery or hand-crank radio, ideally a NOAA Weather Radio. It works when the power and cell networks don't.
- Download offline maps of your area and your evacuation route

| Alert | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Watch | Hazardous weather may occur | Get ready: check your kit, charge phones, review the plan |
| Warning | Hazardous weather is occurring, about to occur or very likely | Act now: take shelter or leave, as officials direct |

## Guides by emergency

| If this happens | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| The power goes out | [Power outage checklist](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/power-outage-checklist/): food safety, generators, heat and cold |
| A winter storm is coming | [Winter storm checklist](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-prepare-for-a-winter-storm/): home, pipes and car |
| You have to evacuate | [Bug out bag list](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/bug-out-bag-list/): what to grab for 72 hours |
| The tap water isn't safe | [How to make water safe to drink](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-make-water-safe-to-drink/): boil, bleach or filter |
| You're stranded in the car | [Car emergency kit](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/car-emergency-kit/): what to carry and what to do |
| You're lost or hurt outdoors | [12 survival skills](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/survival-skills/): priorities, signaling, shelter, fire and first aid |

New to all of this? [Prepping for beginners](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/prepping-for-beginners/) spreads the work over four weeks, and the [glossary](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/survival-terms/) explains the terms.

## Keep it up

- Every six months: replace expired food, medicines and batteries, and water you bottled yourself.
- Every year: rethink what your household needs and update the plan and the kit.
- Take a first-aid and CPR class. Supplies run out; skills don't.

## Quick answers

### What is emergency preparedness?

Emergency preparedness means getting ready before a disaster so your household can stay safe and look after itself for several days: knowing your local risks, agreeing on a plan, storing water, food and supplies, and making sure you can receive warnings.

### What are the basic steps of emergency preparedness?

Three steps: make a plan with your household (how you'll get alerts, where you'll shelter, your evacuation route and how you'll reach each other), build a kit with several days of water, food and supplies, and stay informed through phone alerts and a battery or hand-crank radio.

### How do I prepare my family for a disaster?

Talk through a plan together: pick an out-of-town contact everyone can text, choose two meeting places, write phone numbers on paper, plan for children, older relatives, pets and medical needs, and learn how to shut off your water, gas and electricity. Then build a kit and practice the plan once.

### What is the difference between a watch and a warning?

A watch means hazardous weather may occur, so get ready. A warning means it is occurring, about to occur or very likely, so act now. The National Weather Service issues both.

### Do I need to sign up for emergency alerts on my phone?

Not for Wireless Emergency Alerts: they are sent automatically to capable phones, with no sign-up. Check that emergency alerts are turned on in your phone's settings, and sign up separately for your county's local alert system.

### How much water should I store for an emergency?

One gallon per person per day. Store at least 3 days' worth and work toward 2 weeks: 12 gallons covers a family of four for 3 days.

## Sources

- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Make a Plan](https://www.ready.gov/plan)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit](https://www.ready.gov/kit)
- [FEMA: National Risk Index](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/learn-more)
- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)
- [National Weather Service: Wireless Emergency Alerts (PDF)](https://www.weather.gov/media/wrn/WEA_flyer_final.pdf)
- [University of Wisconsin-Madison, The Weather Guys: What is the difference between a warning and a watch?](https://wxguys.ssec.wisc.edu/2014/07/07/what-is-the-difference-between-a-warning-and-a-watch/)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# Emergency kit list: what to put in a home emergency kit

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-kit-list/
Updated: 2026-11-09

An emergency kit, also called a disaster supplies kit, is what your household lives on when the power, water or roads are out. This is FEMA's list in plain words, with what to add for your family and how to keep it ready.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 9, 2026. Checked against FEMA's Ready.gov Build a Kit list and CDC guidance.

The short answer

A home emergency kit needs water (1 gallon per person per day), several days of food that won't spoil, a flashlight, a battery or hand-crank radio, a first-aid kit, extra batteries, a whistle, dust masks, basic tools, a manual can opener, local maps, and a phone charger with a backup battery. Add medicines, glasses, copies of documents, cash, warm bedding, and whatever your children, pets and older relatives need. Keep it in one place and check it every six months.

**Download the checklist (PDF)**Home Emergency Kit Checklist: free to print, share and keep with your kit.

[Print version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/emergency-kit-checklist.pdf)[Phone version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/emergency-kit-checklist-phone.pdf)

## What is an emergency kit?

An emergency kit is a set of supplies that lets your household get by for several days without power, running water, open stores or outside help. FEMA calls it a disaster supplies kit; you'll also see emergency preparedness kit, survival kit and 72-hour kit. They all mean the same thing: the basics, gathered in one place before you need them.

It's a home kit, meant for staying put through a storm, an outage or a boil-water notice. For leaving in a hurry, each person also needs a smaller bag: see our [bug out bag list](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/bug-out-bag-list/).

## The basic emergency kit

This is the Basic Disaster Supplies Kit from FEMA's Ready.gov, item for item.

- Water: 1 gallon per person per day, for several days. For drinking and sanitation. Use our [water calculator](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-water-calculator/) for your household's total.
- Food: at least several days of non-perishable food. Food that needs no fridge and little or no cooking.
- A battery-powered or hand-crank radio, and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert. For warnings and news when phones and power are down.
- A flashlight
- A first-aid kit
- Extra batteries
- A whistle. To signal for help.
- Dust masks. To help filter contaminated air.
- Plastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape. To shelter in place.
- Moist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties. For personal sanitation.
- A wrench or pliers. To turn off utilities.
- A manual can opener
- Local maps. On paper: your phone may be dead or out of signal.
- A cell phone with chargers and a backup battery

## What to add for your household

FEMA's list of additional supplies covers the things that differ from one family to the next.

### Health and hygiene

- Prescription medicines
- Non-prescription medicines: pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids or laxatives
- Prescription glasses and contact lens solution
- Soap, hand sanitizer and disinfecting wipes
- Feminine supplies and personal hygiene items

### Babies, children and pets

- Infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream
- Books, games, puzzles or other activities for children
- Pet food and extra water for your pet

### Documents and money

- Copies of insurance policies, identification and bank account records. Saved electronically, or in a waterproof container you can carry.
- Cash or traveler's checks. Card readers and ATMs need power and a network.
- Paper and pencil

### Warmth, cooking and safety

- A sleeping bag or warm blanket for each person
- A complete change of clothing suited to your climate, and sturdy shoes
- A fire extinguisher
- Matches in a waterproof container
- Mess kits, paper cups, plates, paper towels and plastic utensils

## How much water and food

| Household | Water for 3 days | Water for 2 weeks | Meals for 3 days |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 person | 3 gallons | 14 gallons | 9 |
| 2 people | 6 gallons | 28 gallons | 18 |
| 4 people | 12 gallons | 56 gallons | 36 |
| 6 people | 18 gallons | 84 gallons | 54 |

The table uses 1 gallon per person per day and 3 meals a day. Store more for hot weather, pregnancy, illness and pets. If you run out of stored water, you can make more safe to drink by boiling it or treating it with unscented bleach: our [water guide](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-make-water-safe-to-drink/) has the EPA's doses.

## Keep it ready

- Keep canned food in a cool, dry place
- Store boxed food in tightly closed plastic or metal containers
- Replace expired items as needed
- Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months
- Rethink your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes

## Where to keep kits

| Place | What FEMA suggests |
| --- | --- |
| Home | One designated place, ready in case you have to leave quickly. Make sure everyone in the household knows where it is. |
| Work | Be ready to shelter at work for at least 24 hours: food, water, medicines and comfortable walking shoes, in a grab-and-go case. |
| Car | A kit of emergency supplies in case you're stranded. See our [car emergency kit list](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/car-emergency-kit/). |

## Building a kit on a budget

- Start with what you own: flashlights, blankets, a can opener, a backpack.
- Fill clean, food-grade containers with tap water. It's free.
- Add one or two items to each grocery trip instead of buying everything at once.
- Buy water, medicines and light first. Gadgets can wait.

Our [prepping for beginners](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/prepping-for-beginners/) plan spreads the whole job over four weeks.

## Quick answers

### What should be in an emergency kit?

FEMA's basic kit is water (1 gallon per person per day for several days), several days of non-perishable food, a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio, a flashlight, a first-aid kit, extra batteries, a whistle, dust masks, plastic sheeting with scissors and duct tape, moist towelettes with garbage bags and ties, a wrench or pliers, a manual can opener, local maps, and a cell phone with chargers and a backup battery.

### How much water should be in an emergency kit?

One gallon per person per day, for drinking and sanitation. Store at least 3 days' worth and work toward 2 weeks if you have room: a family of four needs 12 gallons for 3 days and 56 gallons for 2 weeks.

### How many days should an emergency kit last?

FEMA says to plan for several days, and the CDC's water guidance sets 3 days as the minimum and 2 weeks as the goal. Start with 3 days of water and food, then build up.

### What is the difference between an emergency kit and a bug out bag?

An emergency kit stays at home and is for sheltering in place, so it can be large. A bug out bag, or go bag, is a backpack for each person, packed to leave home within minutes and light enough to carry, covering about 72 hours.

### Where should I keep my emergency kit?

In one place at home that everyone in the household knows and can reach quickly. FEMA also suggests a kit at work, ready for at least 24 hours with food, water, medicines and comfortable walking shoes, and a kit in each car in case you're stranded.

### How often should I check my emergency kit?

Look through it every six months: replace expired food and medicines, swap in fresh batteries, and replace water you bottled yourself. Rethink what your household needs once a year, since families change.

## Sources

- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit](https://www.ready.gov/kit)
- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)
- [EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water](https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# How to prepare for a winter storm

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-prepare-for-a-winter-storm/
Updated: 2026-11-05

A winter storm can cut off heat and power for days. Here's what to do before it hits, how to keep pipes from freezing, how to stay warm and safe if the power goes out, and what to keep in the car.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 5, 2026. Checked against Ready.gov, CDC, NHTSA, National Fire Protection Association and American Red Cross guidance.

The short answer

Before a winter storm, gather what you'd need to stay home for several days without power: water, food that needs no cooking, flashlights and batteries, a radio, medicines and warm blankets. Test your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, protect your pipes from freezing, and fill the car's gas tank. During the storm, stay off the roads, never run a generator or grill indoors, and never heat your home with a gas oven or stovetop.

**Download the checklist (PDF)**Winter Storm Checklist: free to print, share and keep with your kit.

[Print version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/winter-storm-checklist.pdf)[Phone version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/winter-storm-checklist-phone.pdf)

## Watch, warning or advisory?

Know the three main winter weather alerts. Sign up for your community's warning system, and keep a NOAA Weather Radio or battery radio in case phones and power go down.

| Alert | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Winter Storm Watch | A blizzard, heavy snow, heavy freezing rain or heavy sleet is possible. Usually issued 12 to 48 hours ahead. |
| Winter Storm Warning | Hazardous winter weather is about to start or has started. Usually issued 12 to 24 hours ahead. Find shelter right away. |
| Winter Weather Advisory | Snow, freezing rain, freezing drizzle or sleet that will cause significant inconveniences, and could become life-threatening if you're not careful. |

## Before the storm: your home checklist

Plan to be on your own for several days. A winter storm can cut off heat, power and phone service, and older adults, children, people who are sick and pets are at greater risk.

- Water: 1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days. The CDC's minimum, for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth. Our [water calculator](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-water-calculator/) works out your total.
- Food that needs no cooking or refrigeration, and a manual can opener
- Flashlights or headlamps and extra batteries. Use flashlights, not candles, in the dark.
- A battery-powered or hand-crank radio, and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert
- Charged power banks and a car phone charger
- Enough prescription medicine to last if you can't get out, plus a first-aid kit
- A warm blanket or sleeping bag for each person, plus hats, gloves and warm layers
- Food and extra water for pets
- Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms with battery backup, tested. Ready.gov lists carbon monoxide poisoning among the main dangers of winter storms.
- Insulation, caulking and weather stripping to keep the cold out
- Know where your main water shut-off valve is. If a pipe bursts, turning off the water fast limits the damage.

Can't afford heating bills or repairs to keep the cold out? The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) can help with heating costs and weatherization.

## How to keep pipes from freezing

Water expands as it freezes, and the pressure can split metal or plastic pipes. Pipes freeze most often where they're exposed to cold: outdoor hose bibs, pool and sprinkler lines, pipes in unheated basements, crawl spaces, attics, garages and kitchen cabinets, and pipes along outside walls with little insulation.

### Before cold weather

- Disconnect, drain and store garden hoses
- Close the inside valves that feed outdoor faucets, then open the outdoor faucets so they can drain. Leave them open, so any water left in the pipe can expand without breaking it.
- Drain pool and sprinkler supply lines the way the manufacturer or installer says, without adding antifreeze unless they tell you to. Antifreeze is dangerous to people, pets and wildlife.
- Insulate attics, basements and crawl spaces
- Wrap exposed pipes with pipe sleeves or UL-listed heat tape or heat cable. Even ¼ inch of newspaper gives some protection where freezes are rare and short.

### On very cold nights

- Let cold water drip from faucets served by exposed pipes. Even a trickle of moving water helps stop a pipe freezing.
- Open the cabinet doors under kitchen and bathroom sinks, after moving cleaners and chemicals out of children's reach. Warm air reaches the pipes.
- Keep the garage door closed if water lines run through the garage
- Keep the thermostat at the same temperature day and night
- Going away? Leave the heat on, set no lower than 55°F

### If a pipe freezes

Only a trickle from the faucet usually means a frozen pipe, often along an outside wall or where the water line comes in through the foundation.

1. Keep the faucet open. Running water helps melt the ice as it thaws.
2. Warm that section of pipe with an electric heating pad wrapped around it, a hair dryer, a space heater kept away from anything that can burn, or towels soaked in hot water.
3. Keep warming it until full water pressure comes back, then check your other faucets: if one pipe froze, others may have too.
4. Call a licensed plumber if you can't find or reach the frozen section, or can't thaw it.

**Never thaw a pipe with an open flame.** Don't use a blowtorch, a kerosene or propane heater, a charcoal stove or any other open-flame device.

## If the power goes out in the cold

**Carbon monoxide is one of a winter storm's biggest dangers.** Use generators and grills only outdoors, and never heat your home with a gas stovetop or oven. If the carbon monoxide alarm sounds, or anyone has a headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea or confusion, get everyone into fresh air right away, then call 911. People who are asleep can die before they notice anything.

- Run a generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages, and let it cool before refueling.
- Keep space heaters at least 3 feet from anything that can burn, and turn them off when you leave the room or go to bed.
- Use the blankets or sleeping bags from your kit, and dress in warm layers.
- If you can't keep warm at home, go somewhere with heat, such as a warming center.

Our [power outage checklist](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/power-outage-checklist/) covers the rest, including how to keep one room warm and how long food in the fridge and freezer stays safe.

## Frostbite and hypothermia: the signs

Limit time outside, and wear layers when you go out. Watch everyone for these signs, especially older adults and children.

| Condition | Signs | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypothermia | Shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech or drowsiness. A body temperature below 95°F is an emergency: call 911. | Get to a warm room. Warm the center of the body first: chest, neck, head and groin. Keep the person dry and wrapped in warm blankets, including the head and neck. |
| Frostbite | Numbness, and white or grayish-yellow skin that feels firm or waxy, usually on the face, fingers or toes. | Get to a warm room. Soak the area in warm water, or warm it with body heat. Don't massage it or use a heating pad. |

Shoveling snow is hard work, and overexertion raises the risk of a heart attack. Take it slowly and rest often.

## Driving and your car

- **Stay off the roads** if you can. Check the forecast and road conditions before any trip.
- **Keep the gas tank full,** or an electric car charged. A full tank also keeps the fuel line from freezing.
- **Pack a winter car kit:** a shovel, ice scraper, sand or kitty litter, jumper cables, a flashlight, blankets and warm clothes, water, snacks and a phone charger. Our [car emergency kit list](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/car-emergency-kit/) has the full checklist.
- **If you're stranded, stay with the car.** Tie something bright to the antenna or a window, and keep the dome light on. Clear snow from the exhaust pipe, and run the engine only now and then, just long enough to stay warm. Don't run it for long with the windows up or in an enclosed space.

## Quick answers

### How do you prepare for a winter storm?

Get supplies to stay home for several days without power: water (1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days), food that needs no cooking, flashlights and extra batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, medicines and warm blankets. Test your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, protect pipes from freezing, fill your car's gas tank, and plan to stay off the roads.

### How do I keep my pipes from freezing?

On very cold nights, let cold water drip from faucets served by exposed pipes, open the cabinet doors under sinks, keep the garage door closed, and keep the thermostat at the same temperature day and night, the American Red Cross advises. Before winter, insulate exposed pipes and drain outdoor hoses. If you go away, leave the heat on at 55°F or higher.

### What is the difference between a winter storm watch and a warning?

A winter storm watch means a blizzard, heavy snow, heavy freezing rain or heavy sleet is possible, usually 12 to 48 hours ahead. A winter storm warning means hazardous winter weather is about to start or has started, and is usually issued 12 to 24 hours ahead. Under a warning, Ready.gov says to find shelter right away.

### What temperature should I keep my house to stop pipes freezing?

If you'll be away in cold weather, the American Red Cross says to leave the heat on and set no lower than 55°F. While you're home, keep the thermostat at the same temperature day and night instead of turning it down overnight.

### Can I use my gas oven to heat the house if the power goes out?

No. Ready.gov says never to heat your home with a gas stovetop or oven: it can cause carbon monoxide poisoning and fires. Use generators and grills outdoors only, and keep battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms near every sleeping area.

## Sources

- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Winter Weather](https://www.ready.gov/winter-weather)
- [American Red Cross: Preventing and Thawing Frozen Pipes](https://www.redcross.org/get-help/how-to-prepare-for-emergencies/types-of-emergencies/winter-storm/frozen-pipes.html)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit](https://www.ready.gov/kit)
- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)
- [CDC: About Carbon Monoxide Poisoning](https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html)
- [CDC: Prevent Carbon Monoxide Poisoning](https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/psa-toolkit/prevent-carbon-monoxide-poisoning.html)
- [National Fire Protection Association: Heating safety](https://www.nfpa.org/education-and-research/home-fire-safety/heating)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Power Outages](https://www.ready.gov/power-outages)
- [NHTSA: Winter Weather Driving Tips](https://www.nhtsa.gov/winter-driving-tips)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# Car emergency kit: what to keep in your car

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/car-emergency-kit/
Updated: 2026-11-05

Breakdowns, storms and long closures happen far from home. Here's what to keep in the car year-round, what to add for winter, how to check the car before you go, and what to do if you're stuck.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 5, 2026. Checked against NHTSA and Ready.gov guidance.

The short answer

Keep jumper cables, a flashlight, flares or reflective triangles, a first-aid kit, a phone charger, a blanket, water and snacks, and a paper map in the car all year. For winter, add a snow shovel, an ice scraper, sand or kitty litter, and warm clothes, and keep the gas tank close to full. If you're stranded, stay with the car.

**Download the checklist (PDF)**Car Emergency Kit Checklist: free to print, share and keep with your kit.

[Print version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/car-emergency-kit-checklist.pdf)[Phone version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/car-emergency-kit-checklist-phone.pdf)

## The car emergency kit checklist

Adapted from NHTSA's and Ready.gov's lists. Pack them in a bag or bin that stays in the trunk.

### Safety and repair

- Jumper cables. Cold weather drains batteries. In the cold, engines need more battery power to start.
- Flashlight, plus extra batteries
- Flares, reflective triangles or other emergency markers
- A whistle, to signal for help
- A paper map of the area. Phones die and lose signal.

### First aid and comfort

- A first-aid kit, including a tourniquet. NHTSA's list includes a tourniquet. Learn to use one in a Stop the Bleed® class.
- Any medicines you or your passengers need
- Bottled water
- Non-perishable snacks
- A blanket
- A phone and a car charger

### Winter add-ons

- A snow shovel, broom and ice scraper
- Sand or kitty litter. Pour it under the tires for traction if you get stuck.
- Extra blankets and warm clothes: hats, gloves and dry socks
- Winter washer fluid with de-icer, with the reservoir full. One snowstorm can use a lot of it.

Keep the gas tank close to full whenever you can, or an electric car charged. A full tank helps in an evacuation or a power outage, and it keeps the fuel line from freezing.

## Check the car before winter

| Check | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Tire pressure | Pressure drops as it gets colder. Inflate to the number on the label in the driver's door frame, not the maximum printed on the tire, and check when the tires haven't been driven for at least 3 hours. |
| Tread | At least 2/32 of an inch. Put a penny in the tread with Lincoln's head upside down: if you can see the top of his head, replace the tire. Consider winter tires, or chains or studs where they're required. |
| Battery | Have a mechanic check the battery, charging system and belts. Electric and hybrid cars lose range in the cold. |
| Lights and wipers | Check headlights, brake lights, turn signals and flashers. Test the defroster and replace worn wiper blades. |
| Coolant | Enough coolant (antifreeze) that meets your owner's manual, with no leaks. |
| Recalls | Look up your vehicle on NHTSA's recall lookup. Recall repairs are free. |

## If you're stranded

1. **Call 911** if you're in danger or someone is hurt.
2. **Stay in the car.** It's your shelter. Don't wear yourself out.
3. **Make the car visible.** Put something bright on the antenna or in a window, and keep the dome light on.
4. **Prevent carbon monoxide poisoning.** Clear snow from the exhaust pipe, and run the engine only now and then, just long enough to stay warm. Don't run it for long with the windows up or in an enclosed space.
5. **Stay warm.** Use the blankets and warm clothes in your kit.

## Kids, car seats and winter coats

A bulky coat can stop a car seat harness from fitting snugly. Dress children in thin, warm layers, buckle the harness snug, then put a blanket or their coat over the top.

## Other kits to keep

Ready.gov suggests supplies for home, work and the car, since you don't know where you'll be when something happens. Our [bug out bag list](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/bug-out-bag-list/) covers a 72-hour bag for evacuations, and the [winter storm checklist](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-prepare-for-a-winter-storm/) covers the house.

STOP THE BLEED® is a registered trademark of the U.S. Department of Defense.

## Quick answers

### What should be in a car emergency kit?

Jumper cables, a flashlight, flares or reflective triangles, a first-aid kit (NHTSA suggests one that includes a tourniquet) and any medicines you need, a phone car charger, a blanket, bottled water, non-perishable snacks and a paper map. In winter, add a snow shovel, broom and ice scraper, sand or kitty litter for traction, and warm clothes.

### What should I keep in my car in winter?

A snow shovel, broom and ice scraper, sand or kitty litter in case you get stuck, blankets and warm clothes, a flashlight, jumper cables, water and snacks, and a phone charger. Keep the gas tank close to full, or an electric car charged, and fill the washer fluid with winter fluid that has de-icer.

### What do you do if you get stranded in your car in a snowstorm?

Stay with the car and don't overexert yourself. Make it visible with something bright on the antenna or a window and the dome light on. Clear snow from the exhaust pipe, and run the engine only now and then, just long enough to stay warm. Don't run it for long with the windows up or in an enclosed space.

### How do I check if my tires are safe for winter?

Inflate them to the pressure on the label in the driver's door frame, not the number on the tire, and check when the tires are cold. Tread should be at least 2/32 of an inch: put a penny in the tread with Lincoln's head upside down, and if you can see the top of his head, it's time for new tires.

## Sources

- [NHTSA: Winter Weather Driving Tips](https://www.nhtsa.gov/winter-driving-tips)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Car Safety](https://www.ready.gov/car)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Winter Weather](https://www.ready.gov/winter-weather)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit](https://www.ready.gov/kit)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# Bug out bag list: what to pack for 72 hours

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/bug-out-bag-list/
Updated: 2026-11-03

A bug out bag is a pack you can grab in minutes when you have to leave home fast. This checklist covers what goes in it, how much water and food to carry, and how to keep it ready.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 3, 2026. Checked against FEMA's Ready.gov kit list, CDC and National Park Service guidance.

The short answer

Pack enough to get each person through 72 hours on their own: drinking water and a way to purify more, three days of food that needs no cooking, a flashlight, a radio, a first-aid kit and your medicines, a whistle, masks, warm layers and rain gear, a phone charger and power bank, copies of your IDs and some cash, plus anything your kids, pets or older relatives need. Keep one bag per person by the door and check it every six months.

**Download the checklist (PDF)**72-Hour Bug Out Bag Checklist: free to print, share and keep with your kit.

[Print version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/72-hour-bug-out-bag-checklist.pdf)[Phone version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/72-hour-bug-out-bag-checklist-phone.pdf)

## What is a bug out bag?

A bug out bag, also called a go bag, grab-and-go bag or 72-hour kit, is a backpack packed in advance so you can leave home within minutes during a wildfire, flood, hurricane evacuation, gas leak or house fire. The idea comes from the assumption FEMA builds its own kit list on: in a disaster, help may not reach you for several days, so you should be able to take care of yourself until it does.

It is different from the supplies you keep at home. A home kit is for sheltering in place and can be large: two weeks of water and food if you have the space. A bug out bag has to be light enough to carry, so it covers the essentials for about three days and relies on a way to purify water rather than carrying all of it.

## The bug out bag checklist

Work through it category by category. Print the page to tick items off as you pack.

### Water

- Water bottles or a hydration bladder, 2 to 3 liters per person. A gallon of water weighs about 8.3 pounds, so carry some and plan to purify the rest.
- A way to make water safe: a portable filter plus purification tablets, or plain unscented bleach and a dropper. Most portable filters don't remove viruses, so pair a filter with tablets or bleach.
- A collapsible water container for collecting and treating water

### Food

- Three days of food that needs no cooking: energy or protein bars, nut butter packets, jerky, dried fruit, nuts, ready-to-eat meals
- A manual can opener if you pack any cans, and a spoon
- Food for special diets, babies and pets

### Shelter and warmth

- An emergency blanket or bivy sack
- A rain poncho or rain jacket
- A warm layer and a hat, even in summer
- A sleeping bag or warm blanket if you can carry it
- Work gloves

### Light, power and communication

- A flashlight or headlamp, plus extra batteries
- A battery-powered or hand-crank radio, ideally a NOAA Weather Radio
- A whistle to signal for help. Three blasts is the distress signal, and a whistle carries much farther than your voice.
- A phone charging cable and a charged power bank
- A written list of phone numbers and a paper map of your area. Your phone may be dead or out of signal when you need them.

### First aid and health

- A first-aid kit: bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, and a tourniquet if you know how to use one
- Prescription medicines, with a written list of names and doses
- Over-the-counter basics: pain reliever, antihistamine, anti-diarrhea medicine
- Glasses or contact lenses and solution
- N95 or dust masks. For smoke, ash and dust after fires, storms and earthquakes.
- Hand sanitizer and moist towelettes

### Tools

- A multi-tool or knife
- Matches in a waterproof container and a lighter
- Duct tape and a length of cord
- A wrench or pliers to turn off utilities

### Documents and money

- Copies of IDs, insurance policies and prescriptions in a waterproof bag
- Cash in small bills. Card readers and ATMs need power and a network.
- Emergency contacts, including someone out of town

### Clothing and hygiene

- A complete change of clothes and sturdy shoes
- Extra socks
- Toilet paper, garbage bags and plastic ties for sanitation
- Toothbrush, soap and feminine supplies

### For the people and pets who depend on you

- Babies: formula, bottles, diapers, wipes
- Older adults: hearing aid batteries, mobility aids, extra glasses
- Pets: food, water, leash or carrier, and vaccination records

## How much water and food to pack

FEMA and the CDC both plan around one gallon of water per person per day, for drinking, cooking and hygiene. For 72 hours that's three gallons each, about 25 pounds, which is too heavy for most people to carry far. That's why a bug out bag carries a few liters and the means to treat more.

| Supply | Per person | How to carry it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water | 1 gallon a day (3 gallons for 72 hours) | 2 to 3 liters in the bag, the rest treated on the way or kept in the car |
| Food | 3 days | Calorie-dense, no-cook food. Food labels use 2,000 calories a day as a reference. |
| Medicines | Enough to last until you can reach a pharmacy | In original bottles, with a written list of doses |

To treat water on the move, a rolling boil for one minute is the most reliable method. Without a stove, use bleach: the EPA's dose is 8 drops of 6% unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25% bleach), doubled for cloudy water, then a 30-minute wait. Our [guide to making water safe to drink](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-make-water-safe-to-drink/) has the full table.

## Choosing the bag

- **A backpack, not a duffel.** You may have to walk. Padded shoulder straps and a hip belt make a loaded pack bearable.
- **Light enough to walk a few miles with.** Pack it, put it on, and walk around the block. If that's hard, take things out.
- **Waterproof inside.** Line the bag with a heavy garbage bag and keep documents, medicines and electronics in zip-top bags.
- **Plain-looking.** A bag that looks ordinary is less likely to attract attention in a crowded shelter.

## Where to keep it and when to check it

- **At home:** by the door you'd leave through, or in a hall closet, where everyone in the house knows to find it.
- **In the car:** a smaller kit with water, snacks, a blanket, a flashlight and a first-aid kit, in case you're stranded.
- **At work:** FEMA suggests being ready to shelter there for at least 24 hours, with food, water, medicines and comfortable walking shoes.

Check the bag every six months. Replace water you bottled yourself (the CDC says every six months), rotate food before it expires, swap in fresh batteries, update medicines and clothes for the season, and reassess what your family needs once a year.

## Bug out bag, home kit or get-home bag?

| Kit | For | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bug out bag (go bag) | Leaving home fast in an evacuation | About 72 hours, carried on your back |
| Home kit | Sheltering in place through an outage or storm | At least 3 days, ideally 2 weeks of water and food |
| Get-home bag | Getting from work or the car back home | About 24 hours: water, snacks, walking shoes, light, layers |

## Common bug out bag mistakes

- **Packing too heavy.** A 50-pound bag you can't carry is worse than a 20-pound bag you can.
- **One bag for the whole family.** Each person who can carry a pack should have one, so splitting up doesn't leave anyone without water or medicine.
- **Forgetting medicines and glasses.** They're the hardest things to replace in a disaster.
- **No cash and no paper.** Plan for a dead phone: written phone numbers, a paper map and small bills.
- **Packing and forgetting.** Dead batteries and expired food are common. Put the six-month check on your calendar.
- **Never practicing.** Walk your evacuation route once with the bag on, and make sure everyone knows where the bags are.

## Quick answers

### What should be in a bug out bag?

Water and a way to purify more, three days of food that needs no cooking, a flashlight and a battery or hand-crank radio, a first-aid kit and your medicines, a whistle, masks, warm layers and rain gear, a phone charger and power bank, copies of your IDs, cash in small bills, and supplies for any children, older adults or pets.

### How much water should you pack in a bug out bag?

Plan on 1 gallon per person per day, the amount FEMA and the CDC use. Three gallons weighs about 25 pounds, so most people carry 2 to 3 liters plus a filter and tablets or bleach to treat more.

### Is a go bag the same as a bug out bag?

Yes. Go bag, bug out bag, grab-and-go bag and 72-hour kit all mean a pack you can grab in minutes when you have to leave. A home kit is the larger supply for sheltering in place, ideally two weeks of water and food.

### How often should you check a bug out bag?

Every six months: replace water you bottled yourself, rotate food before it expires, swap in fresh batteries, update medicines and seasonal clothes, and reassess what your household needs once a year.

## Sources

- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit](https://www.ready.gov/kit)
- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)
- [EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water](https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water)
- [National Park Service: The Ten Essentials](https://www.nps.gov/articles/10essentials.htm)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# What to do when the power goes out

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/power-outage-checklist/
Updated: 2026-11-03

A step-by-step power outage checklist: the first 15 minutes, keeping food safe, running a generator without risking carbon monoxide, and what to do when the power comes back.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 3, 2026. Checked against Ready.gov, USDA, CDC, OSHA and U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance.

The short answer

1. Check whether it's just your home, then report the outage to your utility.
2. Keep the fridge and freezer closed: food stays safe about 4 hours in the fridge, 48 hours in a full freezer and 24 hours in a half-full one.
3. Use flashlights, not candles, and unplug electronics so a power surge can't damage them.
4. Run generators, grills and camp stoves outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointed away from the house. Never heat your home with a gas oven or stove.
5. If it gets dangerously hot or cold, go somewhere with power, and check on older neighbors.

**Download the checklist (PDF)**Power Outage Checklist: free to print, share and keep with your kit.

[Print version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/power-outage-checklist.pdf)[Phone version](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/assets/pdf/power-outage-checklist-phone.pdf)

## The first 15 minutes

1. **Check if it's only you.** Look at your breaker panel and whether the neighbors' lights are on. A tripped breaker is a much easier fix.
2. **Report it.** Use your utility's app, website or outage line, and note the estimated restoration time. It tells you whether to plan for hours or days.
3. **Switch to flashlights.** Candles are a fire risk, especially with kids or pets moving around in the dark.
4. **Unplug appliances and electronics.** Power can return with surges that damage them. Leave one lamp switched on so you know when it's back.
5. **Close the fridge and freezer.** Every opening lets cold out. Decide what you need before you open the door.
6. **Save your phone battery.** Turn on Low Power Mode, dim the screen, and text rather than call; texts get through more easily when networks are busy.
7. **Start the backup plan for medical equipment.** If anyone relies on oxygen, a CPAP or refrigerated medicine, act now rather than waiting to see how long the outage lasts.

If you have to drive, treat dark traffic signals as four-way stops.

## Keeping food safe

The USDA's numbers assume the doors stay closed:

| Where | Food stays safe for |
| --- | --- |
| Refrigerator | Up to 4 hours |
| Full freezer | Up to 48 hours |
| Half-full freezer | Up to 24 hours |

- After 4 hours without power, throw out refrigerated meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, soft cheese and leftovers. Ready.gov's rule: discard any perishable food that has been at 40°F or warmer for two hours or more.
- Keep an appliance thermometer in the fridge and freezer so you know the real temperature when the power comes back.
- Frozen food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F or colder can be refrozen or cooked.
- For a long outage, move food to coolers with ice. The USDA says 50 pounds of dry ice should hold an 18-cubic-foot freezer for about 2 days. Don't touch dry ice with bare hands.
- Never taste food to check whether it's safe. When in doubt, throw it out.

## Generators and carbon monoxide

**Carbon monoxide from portable generators alone kills more than 80 people a year in the U.S.**, according to the Consumer Product Safety Commission. It's invisible, has no smell, and builds up from anything that burns fuel. If the carbon monoxide alarm sounds, or anyone has a headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea or confusion, get everyone outside into fresh air right away, then call 911. Several people or pets feeling sick at once is a strong sign.

- Run a generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, the distance the CDC gives, with the exhaust pointed away from the house. Never in a house, garage, basement, crawl space or shed, or on a porch, even with the doors open.
- Never use a grill, camp stove, charcoal or an outdoor propane or kerosene heater indoors, and never heat your home with a gas oven or stovetop.
- Never run a car in a garage, even with the garage door open.
- Put battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide alarms on every level of your home, near bedrooms.
- Never plug a generator into a wall outlet or connect it to your home's wiring without a transfer switch installed by an electrician. OSHA warns this can energize power lines and electrocute utility workers. Otherwise, plug appliances into the generator with heavy-duty outdoor extension cords.

Signs of carbon monoxide poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea or vomiting, chest pain and confusion. People who are asleep or have been drinking can die before they notice anything.

## Staying warm in a winter outage

- Pick one small room, ideally with few windows, and keep everyone in it. Close the doors to other rooms.
- Block drafts under doors with towels, hang blankets over windows at night, and open the curtains on sunny windows during the day.
- Wear loose layers, a hat and dry socks, and share blankets and body heat.
- Eat regular meals and drink warm, non-alcoholic drinks.
- Let faucets drip so pipes don't freeze.
- If you can't keep one room warm, go to a warming center or a home with heat. Babies and older adults lose heat fastest.

## Staying cool in a summer outage

- Spend the hottest hours somewhere with air conditioning: a cooling center, library or store.
- Drink water before you're thirsty, close the blinds on sunny windows, and take cool showers if you still have water.
- Never leave anyone, or a pet, in a parked car.
- Heat stroke is an emergency: a body temperature of 103°F or higher, hot red skin, confusion or passing out. Call 911, move the person somewhere cooler and cool them with cool water or wet cloths while you wait. Don't give them anything to drink.

## Medicines and medical devices

- Talk to your doctor now about a plan for powered equipment and refrigerated medicines.
- Insulin and some other medicines must stay cool but not frozen. The package insert says how long each keeps at room temperature.
- Keep charged backup batteries for oxygen concentrators, CPAPs and power wheelchairs, and know where you'll go if the outage runs long.
- Ask your utility whether it has a medical priority or medical certificate program for customers who depend on electricity.

## When the power comes back

- Wait a few minutes, then plug appliances back in one at a time.
- Check the fridge and freezer thermometers and go through the food rules above before eating anything.
- Reset clocks and alarms, and recharge every battery and power bank.
- Restock whatever you used, so you're ready for the next one.

## Power outage kit checklist

Keep these together where you can find them in the dark.

- A flashlight or headlamp for each person, plus extra batteries
- A battery-powered or hand-crank radio
- Charged power banks and a car phone charger
- Battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms
- Appliance thermometers for the fridge and freezer
- A cooler and frozen ice packs or jugs of frozen water
- Water: 1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days, 2 weeks if you can. The CDC's recommendation. Store more for hot weather, pregnancy, illness and pets.
- At least 3 days of food that needs no cooking, and a manual can opener
- A first-aid kit and a supply of everyone's medicines
- Warm blankets or sleeping bags
- Cash in small bills
- A paper list of phone numbers, including your utility's outage line
- A generator only if you can run it outdoors, at least 20 feet from the house, with the right cords

## Quick answers

### How long does food last in the fridge when the power goes out?

About 4 hours if you keep the door closed. A full freezer keeps food safe for about 48 hours and a half-full one for about 24 hours, according to the USDA. Throw out perishable food that has been at 40°F or warmer for two hours or more.

### How far from the house should a generator be?

Outdoors and at least 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, the distance the CDC gives, with the exhaust pointed away from the house. Never run one in a house, garage, basement, shed or on a porch, even with the doors open.

### What should you not do during a power outage?

Don't run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors or in a garage, don't heat your home with a gas oven or stove, don't connect a generator to your home's wiring without a transfer switch, don't open the fridge more than you need to, and use flashlights rather than candles.

### What should be in a power outage kit?

Flashlights and extra batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, charged power banks, battery-powered carbon monoxide alarms, appliance thermometers, a cooler, water (1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days), no-cook food, a first-aid kit and medicines, warm blankets and some cash.

## Sources

- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Power Outages](https://www.ready.gov/power-outages)
- [USDA: Food safety during a power outage](https://www.usda.gov/node/44742)
- [CDC: About Carbon Monoxide Poisoning](https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html)
- [CDC: Prevent Carbon Monoxide Poisoning](https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/psa-toolkit/prevent-carbon-monoxide-poisoning.html)
- [U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission: What to Know About Generators (PDF)](https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/468_WhattoKnowGenerators_2022_v5.pdf)
- [OSHA: Using Portable Generators Safely (PDF)](https://www.osha.gov/Publications/OSHA3286.pdf)
- [CDC: Heat-Related Illnesses (PDF)](https://cdc.gov/natural-disasters/media/pdfs/2026/09/Heat_Related_Illness-NEWLOGO.pdf)
- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# How to make water safe to drink

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-make-water-safe-to-drink/
Updated: 2026-11-03

Boiling, bleach, tablets and filters, with the exact times and doses from the EPA and CDC, plus where to find water in the wild and at home, and how much to store.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 3, 2026. Checked against EPA, CDC and Minnesota Department of Health guidance.

The short answer

**Boil it.** Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes at high elevation, then let it cool covered. **If you can't boil it,** use plain unscented bleach: 8 drops per gallon of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach, doubled if the water is cloudy. Stir and wait 30 minutes. If the water is cloudy to begin with, let it settle and pour it through a cloth or coffee filter first.

## Step 1: Clear cloudy water first

Dirt and debris shield germs from heat and chlorine. If the water is cloudy, let it stand until the sediment settles, then pour the clearer water off the top through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter. This doesn't make the water safe, but it makes every method below work better.

## Boiling: the most reliable method

1. Bring the water to a **rolling boil**, the kind that keeps bubbling when you stir it.
2. Keep it boiling for **1 minute**.
3. Let it cool naturally, then store it in clean containers with lids.

### How long to boil water at high elevation

Water boils at a lower temperature higher up, so boil it for **3 minutes** at elevation. The CDC sets that threshold at 6,500 feet; the EPA's page uses 5,000 feet. If you're anywhere in the mountains, 3 minutes covers both.

Boiled water tastes flat. Pouring it back and forth between two clean containers a few times puts air back into it.

## Bleach: how many drops per gallon

Use regular, **unscented** liquid household bleach with no added cleaners, and check the label for its strength (usually 6% or 8.25% sodium hypochlorite). These are the EPA's doses:

| Water | 6% bleach | 8.25% bleach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 quart or liter | 2 drops | 2 drops |
| 1 gallon | 8 drops | 6 drops |
| 2 gallons | 16 drops (1/4 teaspoon) | 12 drops (1/8 teaspoon) |
| 4 gallons | 1/3 teaspoon | 1/4 teaspoon |
| 8 gallons | 2/3 teaspoon | 1/2 teaspoon |

- **Double the dose** if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold.
- Stir and **wait 30 minutes** before drinking.
- The water should smell faintly of chlorine. If it doesn't, add the same dose again and wait another 15 minutes.
- If it tastes too strongly of chlorine, pour it between clean containers and let it stand a few hours.

## Purification tablets and iodine

Chlorine dioxide and other purification tablets are light and easy to carry; follow the dose and wait time on the package, which can be longer for cold or cloudy water.

With 2% tincture of iodine, the EPA's dose is 5 drops per quart or liter (10 drops if the water is cloudy or colored), then a 30-minute wait. The Minnesota Department of Health advises that iodine-treated water isn't recommended for pregnant women, people with thyroid problems or iodine sensitivity, or for continuous use beyond a few weeks.

## Do water filters make water safe?

Most portable filters remove parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium, but the CDC says **most don't remove bacteria or viruses**. Only some purifiers are rated for viruses, so check the label. Look for:

- An absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller (NSF Standard 53 or 58) for parasites
- 0.3 microns or smaller for bacteria

Where viruses are a risk, as with water near people, livestock or sewage, filter first and then boil or disinfect. Don't drink floodwater at all (see below).

## Sunlight as a last resort

With no fuel, bleach or tablets, solar disinfection (SODIS) can help with water that's already clear. Fill clean, clear plastic bottles of 2 liters or less, with the labels removed, three-quarters full, shake them, fill them to the top, and lay them in full sun for **6 hours**, or **2 days** if it's cloudy. It doesn't work on cloudy water, so settle and filter first.

## What none of these methods fix

**Boiling, bleach and filters don't remove fuel, chemicals or salt.** Don't drink water that smells of fuel or chemicals, floodwater that may carry them, or pool and hot tub water. Never drink seawater or urine; they make dehydration worse. Use bottled or stored water instead.

## Finding water in the wild

- **Follow the land downhill.** Valleys, green vegetation and animal trails that come together often lead to water.
- **Dig in a dry streambed** at its lowest point. Water may sit just below the surface.
- **Catch rain** with a tarp, poncho or any clean container.
- **Collect dew** before sunrise by walking through grass with cloth tied around your ankles, then wringing it out.
- **Melt snow or ice** before you drink it. Eating snow chills you.

The CDC says to treat all water from outside the home, including rain. If you can't, rain caught directly in a clean container is the lowest-risk source. Clear, fast-moving water is better than stagnant water, but it still needs treating.

## Hidden water at home when the taps stop

- **Your water heater:** turn off its power or gas and close the cold-water valve at the top of the tank, open a hot tap somewhere in the house, and drain water from the valve at the bottom; it may be hot. Refill the tank before turning the power or gas back on. Never use water from a home-heating boiler or radiator.
- **The toilet tank,** not the bowl, if you don't use tank cleaners. Treat it before drinking.
- **Ice cubes** in the freezer.

Use pool or hot tub water for flushing and washing only.

## How much water to store

- At least 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days. The CDC's minimum. A family of four needs 12 gallons.
- A 2-week supply if you have the space
- Extra for hot climates, pregnancy, illness and pets
- Store-bought water: replace it by its expiration date
- Water you bottle yourself: replace it every 6 months

Use food-grade containers with tight lids, and never ones that held chemicals like bleach or pesticides. To sanitize a container, wash and rinse it, swirl in a solution of 1 teaspoon of unscented bleach per quart of water so it touches every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out and let the container air-dry before filling it.

## Quick answers

### How long do you boil water to make it safe to drink?

Bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute. At high elevation, boil it for 3 minutes: the CDC applies this above 6,500 feet and the EPA above 5,000 feet.

### How much bleach do you put in a gallon of water to purify it?

The EPA's dose is 8 drops of 6% unscented household bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach, per gallon. Double it if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold, stir, and wait 30 minutes before drinking.

### Do water filters remove viruses?

Most portable filters don't. The CDC says most remove parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium but not bacteria or viruses; filters with an absolute pore size of 0.3 microns or smaller also remove bacteria, and only some purifiers are rated for viruses. Filter first, then boil or disinfect.

### How much water should you store for an emergency?

At least 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days, and a 2-week supply if you can, according to the CDC. Store more for hot climates, pregnancy, illness and pets, and replace water you bottle yourself every 6 months.

## Sources

- [EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water](https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water)
- [CDC: How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency](https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-find-clean-water-in-an-emergency.html)
- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)
- [CDC: Water Treatment Options When Hiking, Camping or Traveling](https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/prevention/water-treatment-hiking-camping-traveling.html)
- [Minnesota Department of Health: Backcountry Water Treatment](https://www.health.state.mn.us/diseases/waterborne/prevention/backcountry.html)
- [Newcastle University: Solar Disinfection (disaster relief)](https://research.ncl.ac.uk/waterqualitymaps/treatmentmethods/disasterrelief/solardisinfection)
- U.S. Army FM 21-76, Survival: water procurement (in the BugOut library)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.

# Emergency water calculator: how much water and food to store

URL: https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/emergency-water-calculator/
Updated: 2026-11-05

Enter how many people live with you and how long you want to be ready for. The calculator uses the CDC's rule of 1 gallon per person per day, and turns it into jugs, bottle cases and meals.

By the BugOut team. Updated November 5, 2026. Checked against CDC and Ready.gov guidance.

## How the calculator works

- **Water:** 1 gallon per person per day, the CDC's minimum, for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth. Ready.gov notes that a normally active person needs about three-quarters of a gallon of fluid a day, and that needs vary with age, health, activity, diet and climate.
- **Hot weather:** Ready.gov says water needs can double in very hot temperatures, so the box doubles the total.
- **Food:** 3 meals per person per day, from food that won't spoil without a fridge and needs little or no cooking.
- **Bottles:** a case of 24 half-liter (16.9 oz) bottles holds about 3.2 gallons.

Add extra for children, pregnant women, nursing mothers, people who are sick and pets, who may need more, and for any medical needs.

## How to store it

- Buy sealed bottled water and keep it in a cool, dark place. It lasts until the expiration date on the label.
- Or fill your own food-grade containers from a treated tap. Never reuse containers that held chemicals, such as bleach or pesticides.
- Sanitize them before filling: wash and rinse, swirl in 1 teaspoon of unscented bleach per quart of water so it touches every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, then pour it out and let the container air-dry. This solution is for cleaning containers only. Never drink it.
- Label each container with the date you filled it
- Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months

## If you run short

- Don't ration drinking water unless officials tell you to. Drink what you need today and look for more for tomorrow.
- Cut how much your body needs by resting and staying cool.
- Skip alcohol and caffeinated drinks: they make dehydration worse.
- Your water heater tank holds usable water, and so does the toilet tank (not the bowl) if the water is clear and hasn't been treated with toilet cleaners. Our [water guide](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/how-to-make-water-safe-to-drink/) shows how to get it out and how to treat any water you're unsure of.

## The food side

FEMA suggests at least several days of non-perishable food. Store what your household already eats: canned meat, fish, beans, soup, fruit and vegetables, peanut butter, crackers, cereal, nuts and shelf-stable milk, plus a manual can opener. Put new cans at the back and use the oldest first. Our [prepping for beginners](https://jaechung-glitch.github.io/bugout/guides/prepping-for-beginners/) guide has a full list.

## Quick answers

### How much water should I store for an emergency?

At least 1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days, the CDC's minimum, for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth. A 2-week supply is better if you have the space. Store more for hot weather, which can double the water people need, and for children, pregnant women, nursing mothers, people who are sick, and pets.

### How much water does a family of 4 need for 2 weeks?

56 gallons: 4 people × 14 days × 1 gallon. That's 56 one-gallon jugs, or about 18 cases of 24 half-liter bottles. In very hot weather, plan for up to twice as much.

### How long does stored water last?

Store-bought bottled water lasts until its expiration date if it stays sealed in a cool, dark place. Water you bottle yourself in clean, food-grade containers should be replaced every 6 months.

## Sources

- [CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply](https://cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Water](https://www.ready.gov/water)
- [Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit](https://www.ready.gov/kit)

This guide is general safety information, not medical advice or a substitute for training. Guidance changes; check your local emergency management office for advice specific to where you live. In an emergency, call 911.
